audience: Engineers who know APIs and databases and need practical system-design reasoning about caches. Answers should explain what happens, who does the work, and what can go wrong in plain English.
prerequisites: An API handler can read and write records in a database.
Several application instances can handle requests at the same time.
Latency is the time a request takes; a system has limited processing capacity.
A database commit makes a completed write available to subsequent database reads in these scenarios.

slides.title: Stop repeating the same product lookup
paragraphs: A popular product page keeps asking the API for the same name, description, and price. Each request repeats a database lookup.

paragraphs.label: Cache
paragraphs.text: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.

paragraphs: Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write.
In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the product.
slides.remember: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.

slides.title: The same request can take two paths

paragraphs.label: Cache hit
paragraphs.text: The API finds product:42 in the cache and returns its stored details.

paragraphs.label: Cache miss
paragraphs.text: The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.

paragraphs: A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
slides.remember: A hit avoids this database lookup. A miss still needs the database.

slides.title: The application manages the cached copy

paragraphs.label: Cache-aside
paragraphs.text: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.

paragraphs.label: Cache key
paragraphs.text: Identifies the result to reuse. product:42 works for shared product details; prices in different currencies need distinct keys, such as product:42:USD.

paragraphs: Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.
slides.remember: Define what the key identifies, who fills it, and where the authoritative data lives.

slides.title: The price changed. What does the next reader see?
paragraphs: A seller changes the price from $20 to $25. The cached $20 is now stale.

paragraphs.label: Invalidation
paragraphs.text: Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.

paragraphs: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
slides.remember: Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

questions.question: An API caches the dispatch contact for a delivery depot. Its writer commits a new contact to the database and then deletes the cached contact. Follow this exact order: reader R misses the cache, reads the old contact, and pauses; writer W commits the new contact and deletes the key; R resumes and caches the old contact it already read; reader S checks that key. No other operations occur. What contact does S receive? Explain why deleting the key did not ensure freshness. If this endpoint must always read the latest committed contact, name a simple way to avoid serving this stale cached copy; no concurrency protocol is needed.
